extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Mathematician; mathematicians and students interested in classical geometry, trigonometry, and probability (problem solvers and contributors to mathematical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Presentation and solution of classical mathematical problems (geometry, trigonometry, probability, and related exercises) intended for publication and/or submission to a mathematical journal. Includes historical notes, problem statements, methods of solution, and invitations for readers to submit improved or novel resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation to publish novel solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I can venture to say, on the part of the Editors, that if any of my readers shall discover euch a solution, the 'Mathematician' will be open to its publication.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal explicitly invites readers to submit new/clean solutions; publication is possible for novel or improved algebraical resolutions of problems. Submissions should present substantive new methods or closed-form resolutions that the editors deem worthy of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit trivial proofs / concision in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The proofs ot these are too simple to need recapItu]ation here.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a result or step is routine or straightforward, it is acceptable in this venue to omit full recapitulation. Authors may summarize or state simple proofs as understood rather than reproducing trivial details, focusing exposition on novel or nontrivial parts of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address existence, multiplicity, and nature of roots/solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion that each unknown will have two values, may give imaginary roots and be insoluble, or may reduce to a lower degree giving fewer solutions; and the statement that the determination of the unknowns is 'always possible' in principle (but possibly difficult algebraically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions should discuss the solvability of the resulting equations (existence/number of real roots, possibility of imaginary roots, degeneracies reducing degree). Authors are expected to note cases where algebraic resolution is hopelessly complicated and to indicate whether a problem is geometrically solvable even when algebraic simplification is intractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of varied solution methods (trigonometric, algebraic, geometric transformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text surveys multiple approaches (Lhuilier's algebraic expansions, continued-fraction representations, trigonometrical methods, transformations to sines/cosines, coordinate/transform methods for surfaces, geometric constructions for intersections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good submission or solution explores different methods as appropriate: direct algebraic manipulation, trigonometric substitutions, geometric constructions, coordinate transformations, or analytic arguments. Preference is given to methods that illuminate structure, yield symmetry, or simplify the problem even if brute-force algebra is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical attribution and literature awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial emphasis on correct historical attribution (e.g., urging Lhuilier's name to be substituted for Carnot in notices of the problem) and references to prior publications (Liverpool SlaJenf, Mechanics' Magazine, Petersburgh Acta, Annales de Mathématiques, Gregory's Examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting solutions or discussions, authors should cite prior work accurately, acknowledge earlier contributors, and place new results in proper historical and bibliographic context.
